title: One Supplier Away
briefing: Valtren buys all its refrigerant and insulated pallet liners from one supplier, Corvane Materials. Credit reports show Corvane's payment days stretching from 30 to 74. Without liners, pharma shipments stop within three weeks.
Tomasz Brennan wants your view before he signs a three-year exclusive deal Corvane is offering at a 12% discount.

context.text: You introduced a second maintenance contractor two years ago; Tomasz admits it saved them during the Kelvarin dispute.
Pellmoor's pharma client now depends on the same liners.

evidence.title: Supplier credit monitoring
evidence.body: Corvane: payment days to its own suppliers up from 30 to 74 in nine months. Credit score fallen two bands. A major customer of Corvane left last quarter.

evidence.title: Dependency analysis
evidence.body: Liners: 100% from Corvane, about 3 weeks' stock. A second supplier exists (Fennick Packaging), 9% more expensive, needs 8 weeks to qualify for pharma use.

evidence.title: Corvane's offer
evidence.body: Three-year exclusivity, 12% discount (saves about 310,000 a year), payment 50% in advance each quarter.

questions.prompt: What does the offer, read with the credit data, suggest?

options.label: Corvane may need cash: the discount and 50% advance payment are consistent with a supplier in financial difficulty
options.feedback: Stretching its own payment terms while asking for advances is a classic distress signal.

options.label: A good deal: lock in the discount
options.feedback: The advance payments would be lost if Corvane fails.

options.label: Nothing in particular
options.feedback: Three distress signals together are not neutral.

options.label: Decline exclusivity and advance payments; qualify Fennick now as a second source, raise liner stock to 8 weeks, and keep buying from Corvane on normal terms
options.feedback: Pays a modest premium to remove a single point of failure before it fails.

options.label: Sign the exclusive deal for the savings
options.feedback: Deepens the dependency on a supplier showing distress, and pre-pays it.

schedules.description: Corvane Materials enters administration; liner deliveries stop

options.label: Move everything to Fennick immediately
options.feedback: Removes Corvane's risk but recreates single sourcing with a supplier not yet qualified for pharma.

questions.prompt: Dual sourcing costs about 90,000 a year. A Corvane failure would cost about 1.9m. At what annual failure probability does dual sourcing pay for itself?

options.label: About 5% (90,000 / 1.9m)
options.feedback: Break-even probability = cost / loss avoided = 4.7%. The credit signals suggest far higher.

options.label: About 50%
options.feedback: That confuses break-even with the chance of failure.

options.label: It never pays: 90,000 is a certain cost
options.feedback: A small certain cost against a large uncertain loss is what resilience costs.

questions.prompt: Tomasz is measured on savings. How do you get him on side?

options.label: Show him the break-even and the supply-continuity risk, and propose that the committee recognise avoided-loss in his targets
options.feedback: Aligns his incentive with the right decision.

options.label: Ask the CEO to overrule him
options.feedback: Wins once, and he will avoid you next time.

options.label: Let him sign for one year as a compromise

questions.prompt: How do you stop the next single-source surprise?

options.label: Lead a supplier criticality review: tier suppliers by impact and substitutability, with credit monitoring and exit plans for tier 1
options.feedback: Turns one lesson into a standing control.

options.label: Handle each case as it comes
options.feedback: Leaves the organisation to rediscover the same risk.

options.label: Ban single sourcing everywhere
options.feedback: Costly and often impossible; focus on critical items.

lesson: Supplier distress shows up in payment terms before it shows in the news. For critical inputs, the cost of a second source is the price of resilience.
